h: Delhi Police, dispensing the Constitution like a digestive powder
dek: Journalist Dilip Khan traces one thread from the truck of stones found near Jantar Mantar to the lathi-wielding crowd of 10 October: the state has begun to share its right to violence with the mob.
ank: journalists detained on 10 October, at least (according to The News Minute)
when Sansad Marg police had already seized the truck of stones (according to Newslaundry)
body: The essay begins with a truck. On 20 July a truck full of stones was found near Jantar Mantar, and in the Delhi High Court Additional Solicitor General S.V. Raju presented it as an argument against the movement. On 28 July Newslaundry showed that the Sansad Marg police had already seized this very truck on 16 July. The DCP admitted as much but said nothing was deliberate. In the Supreme Court, lawyer Vrinda Grover asked how a truck in police custody got there. That question has still not been answered.

For Dilip Khan, 10 October was the next link in the same chain. Section 163 was in force in Delhi that day. A Newslaundry reporter told the police that men with lathis were sitting in a car, and the car was allowed to leave. Videos show certain 'people' telling the police whom to detain and whom to beat. A teenage girl was slapped while the police stood and watched. In Connaught Place a crowd was asking the police to lathi-charge. According to The News Minute, at least 15 journalists were detained that day.

Then the writer opens the Constitution. Article 19 guarantees the freedom to speak and assemble, and 19(3) allows reasonable restrictions on it, provided they apply to everyone equally. If Section 163 applies to protesters but not to a crowd carrying sticks, then, in the author's words, the equality of Article 14 has been 'ground into powder and swallowed'. A policeman has a nameplate on his uniform; the station keeps a daily diary; he can be held to account. A crowd has no name, and so it escapes accountability. The Bajrang Dal and the Vishva Hindu Parishad have denied any plan, and the BJP called the whole day a 'flop show'.

The writer recalls that mob attacks in the presence of police are not new: the same scenes were seen during the farmers' movement, at JNU and at Jamia. He invokes the idea of the Nazi 'dual state', and says plainly that calling the Delhi of 10 October Nazi Germany would be an exaggeration, but that in principle the country is moving in that direction. His last point is the heaviest: the crowd has begun to decide, and when a state shares its right to violence with such people, it weakens its own monopoly.
nazar: This essay is built not from slogans but from dates and documents, and that is its strength. A truck, a car, a slap: three small incidents, but placed side by side they reveal a pattern in which the law is applied selectively.

For Deshkaal, the real question is the one the author raises: accountability. The police can be questioned, in court, through RTI, in Parliament. A crowd cannot. A state that hands its lathi to a nameless crowd takes away the citizen's last route to accountability.
sawal: Who will hold to account a crowd that wears no nameplate?
ref: Section 163, BNSS
A section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita that replaced Section 144 of the old CrPC. Under it a magistrate can bar people from assembling in an area.
Dual state
An idea from German jurist Ernst Fraenkel's 1941 book: in Nazi Germany a 'normative state' ran according to law, while alongside it a 'prerogative state' practised arbitrary violence.

h: Article 19 in a locked-down city
dek: The Leaflet tests the siege of 10 October against the Constitution: an internet shutdown, detentions from inside an aircraft, and the Supreme Court's interim order of 11 October.
photo_note: Delhi Police barricades outside Nirvachan Sadan
body: According to The Leaflet, a website that writes on legal affairs, more than 50,000 security personnel were deployed in Delhi on 10 October to stop the protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, 45 metro stations were shut, trains were cancelled and the internet was switched off. The article recalls that in January 2020 the Supreme Court held that freedom of speech through the internet is part of Article 19.

CJP's Abhijeet Dipke, Ranka and Saurav Das were detained inside the aircraft itself. According to media reports about 7,000 people were detained in Delhi, among them former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee, Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Manik Sarkar. In the article's view the scene recalls the Emergency. It also notes that education minister Dharmendra Pradhan had to resign in July after the NEET protests.

AISA's Neha Bora's slogan, 'let's make this Jantar Mantar', became the signature of the day: wherever they were stopped, they sat down, from INA to Dilli Haat and the Safdarjung flyover. The leaders were released on 11 October; according to the article, on a surety bond of ₹50,000 for one year. Ajinkya Shinde said half the battle had been won, and Dhruv Rathee called the detention a 'kidnapping'. More than 200 alumni of the National Law School, Bengaluru issued a statement. According to the article more than 10,000 people were detained across the country.

On 11 October the Supreme Court issued notice on a contempt petition and sought a reply by Tuesday. The court said the movement of lawyers and journalists must not be stopped, the internet must be restored, barricades reviewed, no illegal detention made outside the Section 163 area, Section 163 notices near courts removed, and every restriction must meet the test of Article 19(2). The article ends with a sentence from Gandhi in Harijan of 23 February 1934, about tyrants and the fear of public opinion.
nazar: The value of this article lies in its list: what exactly the court said on 11 October is recorded in one place. Next week, when compliance with the order is assessed, this list will be the yardstick.

One thing needs attention: there are different claims about the terms of release. The Leaflet speaks of a bond, while according to Aaj Tak's report Abhijeet Dipke says he signed no bond. Deshkaal records both in the name of their sources.
sawal: Why does the freedom the court keeps repeating never reach the street?
ref: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)

The Supreme Court's January 2020 judgment on the internet shutdown in Jammu and Kashmir. The court held that freedom of speech and trade through the internet is constitutionally protected, and that indefinite shutdowns are not permissible.
Article 19(2)

The provision under which the government can impose 'reasonable restrictions' on free speech, on grounds such as the security of the state, public order or contempt of court. Restrictions must be proportionate.

h: The bigger the siege, the smaller the moral authority
dek: Asad Ashraf argues that a government confident of its support does not shut down a city. Detaining thousands of students who questioned the Election Commission has backfired.
body: In Karvaan India, Asad Ashraf says the size of a siege should be read as a countdown. According to the article, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed in Delhi on 10 October, rail and metro services were halted, mobile internet was off in several areas and Jantar Mantar was sealed. Abhijeet Dipke and two associates were taken off a flight from Mumbai and detained. The writer's argument is that a party confident of its support would have let the march reach Jantar Mantar.

The movement took its name from the very remark that called unemployed young people cockroaches. In July the government held talks over the paper leak, and then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. This time the complaint is against the institution that counts the votes, and the answer came as buses and Section 163.

About 13 crore names were struck off in the SIR. The article cites a newspaper investigation according to which two of the three members of the Commission had questioned Gyanesh Kumar. In the writer's view, voters' trust will return only when the list of deleted names is made public. The BJP's Sambit Patra called the protesters 'anarchic elements' and the day a 'flop'. The Supreme Court called the detentions illegal and thousands were released, but with a condition not to breach the peace for a year.

Among the detained was a man on his way to a gurdwara, and several reporters too. Filming officers inside the aircraft, Dipke said he had come to be arrested. The UN human rights office expressed concern, which India's mission in Geneva called interference in internal matters. The article ends with the line that the buses themselves gave the country its answer.
nazar: This article explains the difference between force and authority. Police, buses and barricades are force; authority is the trust that lets a government need them less. The more force it must use, the less trust it shows.

A caution on the numbers of security personnel: The Leaflet writes more than 50,000, this article more than 30,000. Deshkaal keeps both figures in the name of their sources, because the government has given no official number.
sawal: If the list is correct, what is there to fear in making it public?
ref: SIR (Special Intensive Revision)

The Election Commission process in which the voter list is checked afresh and every voter is asked for papers. It is alleged that a large number of names were deleted across the country in this process.
Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR)
The Geneva-based UN body that monitors human rights worldwide and seeks answers from governments.

h: The right to assemble, and the court's half-hearted regret
dek: The Hindu's editorial: the Centre carried out a martial-law-like swoop on a peaceful protest, and the Supreme Court's piecemeal orders failed to restrain it.
body: The Hindu's editorial begins with the basic guarantee the Constitution gives every citizen: the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. CJP, AISA, SFI and AISF had called a peaceful protest on 10 October. In the paper's words, the Centre ordered a countrywide swoop as if martial law were in force.

Trains were cancelled. Journalists, activists, academics and lawyers were assaulted and detained. Many policemen wore no identification badges. The editorial recalls that no one was punished for the excesses of July, including male police personnel assaulting women.

On 9 October the Supreme Court had said there could be no blanket ban on protest. The very next day that is what was done. The editorial's sharpest line is about the court: its piecemeal orders and half-hearted expressions of regret had no restraining effect on the government.

The paper also notes that critics are being branded foreign agents, that the BJP is defending Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and that the Commission has pushed large numbers of people out of the right to vote. In the editorial's view, the relationship between Gyanesh Kumar and the ruling party does not look like that of an ordinary officer and a government.
nazar: When the editorial of one of the country's major newspapers speaks of the Supreme Court's 'half-hearted' regret, it is a comment not only on the government but on the fatigue of institutions.

Rights do not survive by being written on paper. To protect them, court orders must be obeyed, and when they are not, someone must be held accountable. The excesses of July went unpunished; that is why they were repeated in October.
sawal: If a court order is broken the very next day, whose move is next?
ref: Article 19(1)(b)
The constitutional provision that gives all citizens the right to assemble peaceably and without arms.
Martial law
When the army or military officers run the administration in place of civilian authorities and ordinary legal rights are suspended. The editorial uses the term as a comparison.

h: The other side: did the movement weaken on day two?
dek: Anugrah Mishra's analysis in Aaj Tak says there were more police than protesters at Jantar Mantar on Sunday, and attributes this to the issue being in the opposition's hands.
body: Deshkaal carries this Aaj Tak analysis in today's issue as the other side. According to Anugrah Mishra, the government was determined this time not to let July repeat itself. CJP's leaders were detained as soon as they reached Delhi, and the 'Plan B' led by Ajinkya Shinde did not succeed either. According to the article, Jantar Mantar was quiet on Sunday, with more police there than protesters.

The article compares this with July. Then whole families joined the movement, Sonam Wangchuk fasted, there were three rounds of talks with the government, and the education minister's resignation under the pressure of a movement was a first.

Mishra argues that this time the issue, Gyanesh Kumar and 'vote theft', belongs to the opposition. Rahul Gandhi has been raising it for a year, a memorandum has been given to the President and there are plans to approach the Supreme Court. So, as a pressure group, CJP did not get the response it got in July.

At Sunday's press conference Ranka, Saurav Das and Ratna Singh alleged police excesses. According to the article, Abhijeet Dipke has gone to his village after his grandmother's death, and he says he signed no bond.
nazar: This article matters because it asks directly the question the movement's supporters avoid: did the crowd shrink? But a headcount alone says little. On a day when leaders had already been picked up, the metro was shut and Section 163 was in force, reading an empty street as lack of support is an incomplete reading.
Still, one point in the article deserves thought: when an issue becomes a party's issue, others begin to keep their distance. That is the movement's real challenge.
sawal: Is an empty street the absence of anger, or the presence of fear?
ref: CJP
The youth organisation linked to this movement, which called protests in July against the paper leak and in October against the Chief Election Commissioner. Its convenor is Abhijeet Dipke.
Pressure group
An organisation that does not contest elections but tries to influence government policy through agitation, campaigns and public opinion.

h: Wherever the young stand, there is Jantar Mantar
dek: In a conversation with Harkara, senior journalist Shravan Garg says a siege this large is a political failure, not a success, and that the issue is not one officer but the whole power structure.
by: Shravan Garg, in conversation with Nidhish Tyagi
body: Speaking to Nidhish Tyagi in Harkara's 'Deep Dive', senior journalist Shravan Garg sums up 10 October in one sentence: Jantar Mantar is no longer a place; wherever the young stand, that will be Jantar Mantar. In his view the sheer scale of the security arrangements proves political failure, not success.

Garg says this fight is not just about saving Gyanesh Kumar's chair but about saving the whole power structure behind him. It is the failure not of one leader but of the entire system. He stresses that many of these young people come from groups long regarded as BJP supporters.

The conversation turns to the media too. According to Garg, television's credibility is weakening and the message now reaches the young through social media. As he sees it, the real issue is the SIR and the right to vote, not any single officer. He also says the confrontation could affect Parliament, the judiciary and relations between parties.

In the same edition Harkara cites a report by The Hindu's Vijaita Singh in which officials admitted that such a large deployment cannot be sustained for long, that Connaught Place cannot be kept shut forever, and that the solution has to be political. The newsletter speaks of a leaderless crowd, and also records the voice of Khushboo, a law student.
nazar: The weight of Shravan Garg's view is that he looks at this movement beyond one officer. If the young come from the very groups the establishment considered its own, this is not just protest but a relationship breaking.
That officials themselves concede the answer is politics, not policing, is significant in itself. The question is who will take that political initiative, and when.
sawal: When every crossroads becomes Jantar Mantar, how many crossroads can be shut?
ref: Jantar Mantar
An 18th-century astronomical observatory in Delhi; the road beside it has for decades been the designated site for sit-ins and protests.
Harkara
An independent Hindi newsletter that publishes daily news along with conversations under the name 'Deep Dive'.

h: JP at 124: resistance then, and our children now
dek: Dr Suresh Khairnar, former president of the Rashtra Seva Dal, recalls travelling to Delhi with JP's movement in 1974, and sets it against the Delhi of 10 October.
body: 11 October was Jayaprakash Narayan's 124th birth anniversary. To mark it, Dr Suresh Khairnar, former president of the Rashtra Seva Dal, has written a long essay in Countercurrents that is both memoir and comment on today's politics.

The writer recalls the 2023 winter session, when 146 MPs were suspended, 19 bills were passed without debate and the procedure for selecting election commissioners was changed. He claims that 13 crore names were struck off in the SIR and that opposition voters were targeted. (This is the author's claim.) Of 10 October he mentions masked men carrying sticks alongside the heavy security.

Then he goes back to 1974-75. At 21 he went to Delhi by train; the police stood by quietly, and the Ramlila Maidan filled up. JP had appealed to the police not to obey unconstitutional orders, and Indira Gandhi called him a traitor. The writer recalls an argument about 1942 with his Congressman father, and lists JP's Bhoodan work, the surrender of the Chambal dacoits and his diplomacy on the Bangladesh question.

The essay's sharpest line is that Modi is the male edition of Indira Gandhi, with corporate money behind him this time. In the end the writer sees the difference between his generation's resistance and that of 'our children' today: then the police stood and watched; today the road itself is closed.
nazar: Remembering the JP movement is easy; learning from it is hard. The strength of this essay is that it does not turn history into a monument, but presents it as the memory of a living man.

Some of the figures and comparisons in the essay are the author's own opinion and should be read as such. But a question remains: what is the generation that stood against the Emergency of 1975 leaving behind for its children?
sawal: Who inherited JP's legacy, power or the street?
ref: Total Revolution
The call JP gave from Patna's Gandhi Maidan in 1974, for political, economic, social and educational change. This movement later became the centre of opposition to the Emergency.
Rashtra Seva Dal
A socialist volunteer organisation founded in 1941 that works among young people on secular and democratic values.

h: The Red Cross president's warning: we may be in the middle of a third world war
dek: Mirjana Spoljaric, who has been to Gaza and has met the Iranians, tells The New York Times that more wars are being fought today than at any time since the Second World War, and that the rules of war are breaking down.
photo_note: Mirjana Spoljaric, president of the ICRC
body: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) usually works quietly and rarely speaks to the media. That makes this conversation between its president, Mirjana Spoljaric, and Lulu Garcia-Navarro in The New York Times' 'The Interview' unusual. She has been to Gaza, she has met Iranian officials, and what she says carries a warning.

According to Spoljaric, about 130 international and non-international armed conflicts are under way in the world today, the highest number since the Second World War and double the figure of 15 years ago. History will decide, she says, whether we have unknowingly reached the start, or the middle, of a third world war. These wars are no longer separate but form a web, in which Russia, China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen's Houthis and many non-state groups trade weapons and technology.

She charges that leaders have stopped caring about the Geneva Conventions and now claim 'total victory', when there is never total victory in war, only destruction and death. War has become not a route to a political solution but a means of staying in power. When those in power say 'there are no red lines', the message reaches every man who picks up a weapon that he can do whatever he wants.

Of Gaza she says that human dignity there has been stripped away entirely, and that what happened in Gaza and Israel has crossed every legal and moral limit. She speaks of double standards: the humanitarian needs of Europe and those of African or Arab countries are seen through different lenses. The ICRC's access to hostages and prisoners has been made difficult, although under the Geneva Conventions this is the states' obligation. Her final worry is that the world has forgotten how to compromise: jumping into war has become easy, getting out almost impossible.
nazar: When the head of the Red Cross uses words like 'third world war', it is not headline language but the weariness of an institution that counts the dead on every front and asks permission to see prisoners.

This interview should be read in today's issue alongside Navi Pillay's Nobel and the US sanctions on the International Criminal Court. All three say the same thing: the rules and institutions built after the Second World War are crumbling, and saving them is not the responsibility of any one country.
sawal: When leaders say there are no red lines, at what line will a soldier stop?
ref: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)
A neutral humanitarian organisation founded in Geneva in 1863 that helps the wounded, prisoners and civilians in war, and is regarded as the guardian of the Geneva Conventions.
Geneva Conventions
The four treaties of 1949 and later protocols that set the rules for protecting wounded soldiers, prisoners of war and civilians in war. Almost every country is party to them.

h: Navi Pillay's Nobel: a call to return to rules
dek: The Hindu's editorial says this year's peace prize has gone to a judge who held rape to be genocide and spoke of genocide in Gaza, and that this is a message for a world full of wars.
body: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay. She was born in 1941 in Durban into a family of Indian Tamil origin. During apartheid she represented prisoners on Robben Island, Nelson Mandela among them.

At the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the 1998 Akayesu judgment for the first time recognised rape as part of genocide, and Pillay was a judge on that case. Later she chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory, which spoke of genocide in Gaza and said Netanyahu and Gallant had 'incited' it.

The editorial contrasts this choice with the prizes given to Barack Obama in 2009 and María Corina Machado in 2025, which were questioned. This time the prize has gone not to a promise but to decades of work.

The world's picture is dark: the Russia-Ukraine war; Israel's bombing of Gaza, Syria and Lebanon; the US war on Iran since 28 February, in which its Supreme Leader was killed; and US sanctions on the International Criminal Court. In the editorial's view, the prize's message is that rules and institutions must be strengthened.
nazar: In a year when international courts themselves face sanctions, a peace Nobel for an international judge is a statement in itself.
It is a mirror for India too. A woman of Tamil origin who fought prisoners' cases under apartheid is today the symbol of the very justice that powerful countries most dislike.
sawal: When powerful countries sanction the courts themselves, who will set the measure of peace?
ref: Akayesu judgment (1998)
A judgment of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda that convicted local mayor Jean-Paul Akayesu of genocide and, for the first time, recognised rape as an act of genocide.
Robben Island
An island near Cape Town where political prisoners were held during apartheid. Nelson Mandela spent 18 years there.

h: A year of 'ceasefire': Gaza's healthcare is still collapsing
dek: Sally Saleh of Medical Aid for Palestinians says that even after the ceasefire, patients in Gaza are dying while they wait for treatment, because oxygen, machines and spare parts are not being let in.
body: Sally Saleh works with Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) in Gaza. According to her, more than 1,470 people have been killed since the ceasefire. At a MAP centre in Jabalia, a 65-year-old man was killed by quadcopter fire.

Count the needs and the list is long. Amputees need prosthetic limbs, children suffer from anaemia and stunted growth, there is no radiotherapy, and dialysis stops intermittently. The writer tells Iktimal's story: her biopsy was delayed for over a month, it turned out to be cervical cancer, she had surgery in April, her kidneys failed, her evacuation was delayed, and in the end she died in Egypt.

According to the World Health Organization, more than 15,000 people are waiting to leave Gaza for treatment. A newborn with a heart condition died at Assahaba hospital. More than 500 patients depend on oxygen, but 22 of 34 oxygen stations are down and only 4 of 30 filling machines are working. Spare parts are being blocked as 'dual-use' items.
For about 2 million people there is not a single MRI machine, and only one or two CT scanners. The article's last line is simple: Iktimal ran out of time.
nazar: If ceasefire means only that the big bombs have stopped, it is half a word. Death in Gaza has now slowed down: a delayed biopsy, a shut oxygen station, a spare part held at the border.
Countries, India among them, that have welcomed the Gaza ceasefire must ask whether they will demand just as loudly that medicines and machines be let in.
sawal: In a ceasefire where patients die waiting for treatment, whose peace is it?
ref: Dual-use items
Goods that can have both civilian and military uses. On this ground Israel blocks many pieces of equipment and spare parts bound for Gaza.
Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP)
A UK-based humanitarian organisation that works on health services for Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon and elsewhere.

h: How to save the International Criminal Court
dek: Two legal scholars say US sanctions are strangling the court while Europe stays silent for fear of tariffs; the way out lies in budgets, legal shields and alternative banking.
body: US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) mean its assets are being blocked and American companies cannot do business with it. The US has given a 180-day grace period, with licences for salaries, insurance, rent, telecom and cloud services.

According to the writers, this 'grace period' is really coercion. On 10 October Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, said threats were 'not acceptable', but Europe sits on its hands for fear of tariffs.

They fear that in the name of dialogue the court may sacrifice its Palestine investigation. Instead they propose concrete steps: member states should raise the court's budget and pass laws to shield it from sanctions, the EU should activate its Blocking Statute, and separate banking and digital infrastructure should be built for the court.
Their warning is clear: if the ICC falls, no court in the world will be able to work without fear.
nazar: This article is a reminder that international justice runs not only on judges but on bank accounts, servers and insurance policies. Sanctions squeeze exactly these veins.
India is not a member of the ICC, but for countries that speak of a 'rules-based order' this is a test of whether they will defend the rules even when the rules hurt a powerful friend.
sawal: How can a court that fears the powerful give justice to the weak?
ref: Rome Statute
The 1998 treaty that created the International Criminal Court, which tries genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The US, Israel and India are not members.
Blocking Statute
A 1996 EU regulation that forbids European companies from complying with certain foreign sanctions and allows them to recover damages caused by them.

h: Cables under the sea, occupation on land
dek: Alli Armijo shows that the subsea cables and data centres on which the world of AI rests are laid along old imperial routes, oil pipelines and maps of occupation.
body: The world's internet runs on more than 600 subsea cables, over 1.5 million kilometres long. According to the article, Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft own about 75 percent of them, and many cables follow the same routes once used by slave ships and then by oil.

The writer moves from the US Telecommunications Act of 1996 to a new act of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) that names China, Russia, North Korea and Iran. Sea lanes like Hormuz matter as much in this story as they do for oil.

In the Gulf, oil money is now going into data: Saudi Aramco's $4 billion investment, the Gulf states' data centres, Trump's $600 billion deal with Saudi Arabia in 2025, the Saudi AI company HUMAIN, and the partnership with Turing in March 2026.

Israel hosts Amazon, Azure, Google and Oracle data centres, the $9 billion JWCC contract, and the Leviathan gas field. Palestinians have no jurisdiction over their own data. The article ends with Mahmoud Abbas's speech to the UN on 24 September, delivered remotely after he was denied entry: we will not leave our homeland.
nazar: The word 'cloud' creates the illusion that data floats somewhere in the air. This article brings it back to the ground, and to the sea floor, where the owners, the routes and the military contracts are plain to see.
India too is becoming a major hub for data centres and subsea cables. The question is whether our share in this infrastructure will be that of an owner or a tenant.
sawal: Does whoever owns the cable own the truth as well?
ref: JWCC
The US Department of Defense's Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability contract, worth about $9 billion, split among Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle.
Leviathan gas field
A large natural gas reserve in the Mediterranean off Israel's coast, in production since 2019.

h: Rhinos get buffer zones, Kaziranga's Adivasi farmers get the NSA
dek: Shreya Shivam writes that Pranab Doley, who opposed hotel projects near Kaziranga, has been booked under the National Security Act, while the buffer zone is set to shrink.
body: Pranab Doley of the Greater Kaziranga Land and Human Rights Protection Committee was detained on 12 July in connection with a protest on 28 June. He got bail on 29 July, and on 30 July the National Security Act (NSA) was invoked against him. The NSA hearing in the Gauhati High Court has moved from 5 October to 15 October.

The dispute is about hotels. According to the government, a Hyatt-linked hotel is worth ₹100 crore, with 120 rooms, on about 30 acres. Activists say 60 bighas of land at Inlay Pathar are being taken. A ₹120 crore Taj hotel is also proposed at Hatikhuli. Forty-five families are affected, 20 of whom have gone to the High Court.

The Environment Ministry has said in an affidavit that there is no tourism plan. Meanwhile the chief minister wants to cut the buffer zone from 10 km to 1 km, 1 to 3 km depending on the site. More than 60 human rights organisations and UN experts have condemned the detention, and on 24 September 26 indigenous communities held a solidarity rally in Kenya.

There are three demands: make the environmental impact assessment public, demarcate the buffer zone, and review the detention. The article's last line reads like a question: whose heritage is a World Heritage Site that cannot tolerate questions from its own farmers?
nazar: Driving out local people in the name of conservation and then building five-star hotels on the same land is a contradiction repeated in many of the country's forests.
Invoking the NSA the day after bail shows the aim is not to win a case but to keep a man inside. The hearing on 15 October must be watched.
sawal: Rhinos get a buffer zone; what do the farmers who protect them get?
ref: National Security Act (NSA), 1980
Under this law the government can detain a person without trial for up to 12 months if they are deemed a threat to 'public order' or security.
Eco-sensitive zone (buffer zone)
The area around national parks and sanctuaries where mining, large construction and polluting activities are banned or regulated.

h: Surat's Bihari weavers: the fight for an eight-hour shift
dek: Pushyamitra reports that workers from Bihar and UP in Surat's textile mills have held out since August for an eight-hour day, a weekly off and PF-ESI, and talks with the owners are due today.
body: The movement of workers in Surat's textile mills began in Amroli on 16 August. A large share of them are from Bihar. The demands are basic: an eight-hour working day, one paid day off a week, PF, ESI, gratuity and bonus, and an end to arbitrary wage cuts.

The movement has taken several forms. Under the 'Gaon Chalo Andolan' workers were urged to return to their villages, Ajay Dubey asked them to stay united, and at the end of September the deputy labour commissioner issued directions. A protest planned for 1 October was postponed. According to Newslaundry, three FIRs were filed, eight people were arrested and cases were registered against about 500. According to The Times of India, Ajay Dubey was detained.

Union textiles minister Giriraj Singh made an appeal and visited Surat, which he called a 'mini India'. Karunesh Ranpariya of the owners' body TEJAS says the eight-hour day and a paid weekly off are acceptable, but losses of material will be deducted from wages. He accuses the leaders of inciting the workers, and also objects to the use of mobile phones at work.
Talks between workers and owners are due on 12 October. Their outcome was not known when the article was published.
nazar: The eight-hour day is a century-old demand for which workers across the world gave their lives. That it should bring FIRs and detentions in Surat in 2026 shows how fragile the rights of the migrant worker still are.
The condition attached to the owners' 'acceptance' deserves attention: if losses are cut from wages, the eight-hour victory may remain on paper. That is the real question in today's talks.
sawal: In a city called a 'mini India', who decides the rights of the worker from outside?
ref: ESI (Employees' State Insurance)
A scheme under a 1948 law, funded by contributions from both worker and employer, that gives workers medical care, sick leave and help after accidents.
Deputy Labour Commissioner
An officer of the state labour department who enforces labour laws and mediates disputes between workers and employers.

h: Biharis drowning in kalash processions: whose responsibility?
dek: On the first day of Durga Puja, 16 people drowned in Bihar while filling kalash pots. Bihar Chronicle asks who is responsible for accidents that repeat every year.
body: On the first day of Durga Puja, 16 people in Bihar drowned while filling water during kalash processions. According to a compilation by Prabhat Khabar, there were three deaths each in Muzaffarpur, Darbhanga and Sitamarhi, and one each in Samastipur, Sheohar, Bhojpur, Saran, Begusarai, Nawada and Rohtas. In Ramnagar, West Champaran, a flag touched a high-tension wire, killing two children and burning 18 people.

This is not the first time. On Jitiya in 2024, 46 people drowned, 37 of them children. The article lists the causes: SDRF and NDRF are deployed around cities, illegal sand mining has left deep pits in the rivers, and divers are few.

The state has declared drowning a state-specific disaster, and the family of the dead receives ₹4 lakh in compensation. But 'Mission Surakshit Ghat' has not reached the ground, more than 19,000 trained Aapda Mitras are not being used, and the rule of a safety check of the ghats 48 hours in advance exists only on paper.
The article does not put the responsibility on the government alone. Puja committees and parents too must make sure children do not go into deep water unsupervised.
nazar: The ₹4 lakh comes after death, whereas a ghat inspection, a diver and a rope are needed before it. A government that hands out compensation every year but does not inspect the ghats has made the accident a habit.
The mention of pits left by illegal sand mining matters. This is a question not of faith but of a trade that is hollowing out the rivers.
sawal: When will we stop calling these yearly deaths accidents?
ref: SDRF and NDRF
The State and National Disaster Response Forces, which carry out rescue in floods, drownings and other disasters.
Aapda Mitra
Local volunteers trained under a central scheme to provide first response in disasters.

h: Students attacked in Delhi: four Hindutva men arrested
dek: Delhi Police have arrested four men for beating students and pushing women during an anti-SIR protest on DDU Marg.
body: According to Maktoob, Delhi Police have arrested four men for assaulting students and pushing and hitting women during an anti-SIR protest on Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Marg.
Those arrested are Raman Saini (50), Vivekanand alias Vivek (32), Kapil Kumar (27) and Ravinder Singh alias Govind Hindu (35). The Kamla Market police registered the case suo motu.
According to the report, a policeman can also be seen in the video of the attack. The story also records the police's statement as quoted by The Indian Express, and a post by Delhi Police on X.
nazar: The arrests are welcome, but Dilip Khan's essay today is a reminder that the question is bigger than four men: what was the policeman in the video doing at that moment, and how were such groups allowed to roam inside the Section 163 area?
sawal: Who will question the policeman standing in the video?
ref: Suo motu
When the police or a court registers a case on its own, without waiting for a complaint.
DDU Marg
Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Marg in Delhi, where the BJP's national headquarters and several political offices are located.

h: Journalists detained and harassed again on day two
dek: At least 20 journalists covering the anti-SIR protests were detained on 11 October, and Maktoob's women reporters faced religious slurs.
body: According to Maktoob, at least 20 journalists were detained on 11 October, the second day of the protests. Maktoob's Fida Fathima, Nada Saeeda and Aktarista Ansari faced Islamophobic slurs, and Nandini Singh was allegedly groped.

Journalists of Indian Express Hindi were taken to Chhatrasal Stadium. Newslaundry's Nidhi Suresh, Peek TV's Vedanta Agarwal and Sara Khan, and reporters of Malayalam channels were also detained. On Saturday Scroll's Ayush Tiwari and Shoaib Daniyal, and Divya Aslesha in Pune, had been stopped.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) released a list naming at least 16 journalists, including Paranjoy Guha Thakurta. In Ahmedabad, Kinjal of Alt News was detained. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and the United Nations issued statements, which the Ministry of External Affairs called unwarranted.
nazar: Detaining a journalist is detaining the news. On a day when the reporter is not on the street, what happens has no witness.
Religious slurs and molestation directed at women journalists show that the target is not just the press, but a press with a particular identity.
sawal: When the witness is in detention, who will write the truth of the street?
ref: Reporters Without Borders (RSF)
A Paris-based organisation that monitors press freedom worldwide and publishes the annual World Press Freedom Index.
Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)
A New York-based organisation that records attacks, arrests and killings of journalists.

h: Fresh violence in Manipur: nine dead, a dozen houses burnt
dek: Nine people were killed in violence in Kamjong, Kangpokpi and Ukhrul on 9 and 10 October, among them Naga, Kuki and people of Nepali origin. Shutdowns on the highways continue.
body: Nine people were killed in violence in Manipur's Kamjong, Kangpokpi and Ukhrul districts on 9 and 10 October. According to the Hindustan Times count, four, four and one died: six Naga, two Kuki and one of Nepali origin.

Domkhonei Touthang, 42, a mother of five, was killed near Chassad police station. Michael Ngamminlen Haokip, 23, was also killed, and 14 houses were burnt. At Ningchou, Ngachanso Ningshen and Leishisan Leishadang were killed. Sandeep Rai was shot on NH 202. Three Naga village guards were killed at Makui Ashang, and a civilian at Tapon Liangmai.

The Committee on Tribal Unity (CoTU) has called a 24-hour shutdown on NH 2, and there is an indefinite shutdown on NH 202. Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh was meeting Prime Minister Modi at the time. The Kuki Inpi, in a statement, blamed the NSCN-IM.
nazar: While attention is on the streets of Delhi, Manipur is smouldering again, and this time the violence is spreading between Naga and Kuki areas. Three years on, there is still no concrete political initiative to restore trust in the state.
sawal: Why does news from Manipur shrink by the time it reaches Delhi?
ref: NSCN-IM
The National Socialist Council of Nagaland (Isak-Muivah), a Naga armed organisation that has had a ceasefire with the Centre since 1997 and signed a 'Framework Agreement' in 2015.
Kuki Inpi
The apex traditional body of the Kuki community, which puts forward political statements and demands on the community's behalf.

h: Pakistan: emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
dek: President Zardari has imposed an emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on the Sharif government's recommendation. Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and his former ministers are in detention.
body: Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari has imposed an emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on the recommendation of Shehbaz Sharif's cabinet. The province's administration is now in the hands of Governor Faisal Karim Kundi.

The move came in the middle of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi's march towards Islamabad. Gohar Khan, chairman of Imran Khan's party PTI, said talks were deadlocked, and Afridi and members of his former cabinet are in detention. One leader, Bukhari, called it a 'disguised coup' and said that the little democracy that remained is also gone.
In the background is the violence of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) in the province, and containers have been placed in Islamabad to block roads.
nazar: Removing an elected provincial government through an emergency is an old pattern of the grip that the army and the Centre hold on Pakistan's democracy. Containers on the roads and leaders in detention: this picture from next door should not feel unfamiliar to us.
sawal: How much democracy can be suspended in the name of security?
ref: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Pakistan's north-western province on the Afghan border, which has been governed by Imran Khan's party PTI.
Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)
The Pakistani Taliban, an armed group formed in 2007 that attacks the Pakistani army and civilians, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

h: Delhi Deleted: 'We are alive, sir!'
dek: The Red Mike's ground report goes to people in Delhi's SIR who were listed as dead or 'untraceable' in the draft roll, from Lal Gumbad to Bela Ghat and Okhla.
body: The Red Mike's ground report went up on YouTube on 23 September. According to the video's description, about 47.7 lakh of 1.45 crore names were left out of the draft roll in Delhi's SIR, almost every third voter, and more than 33 lakh people received notices for discrepancies or for not being 'mapped'. The Election Commission calls this cleaning up the roll.

The report moves in chapters. In Lal Gumbad in south Delhi, 65-year-old Kunne Lal has lived in the same place for decades but is recorded as dead in the draft. The settlement at Bela Ghat near Chandni Chowk has been uprooted after the bulldozers; according to the video only one name survived out of 729 at one booth. In Okhla people have been marked 'untraceable', and they fear eviction.

Daily wage workers received notices in English, and going to reply costs them a day's earnings. Errors in age and family details are also recorded. The video goes on to the demand raised in the Supreme Court that the names of those served notices, and the reasons, be made public.
The draft is not the final roll: the window for claims and objections is open, and the final roll is due on 4 November.
nazar: Numbers like 13 crore numb us. This report turns them back into faces: an old man who has died on paper, a settlement that has been wiped off the map.
The anger seen on Delhi's streets on 10 October has its roots here. Until the reasons for deleting names are made public, every notice will remain a question.
sawal: Whom should a man killed by paper prove to that he is alive?
ref: Claims and objections
The period after a draft voter roll is published in which anyone can apply to add their name (Form 6) or object to a wrong entry (Form 7).
Bela Ghat
A settlement on the Yamuna bank near Chandni Chowk, where many families were uprooted after a bulldozer drive.

h: Gandhi in Rusnė: a statue of a friendship
dek: Painter-writer Seeraj Saxena reaches a statue of Gandhi and Hermann Kallenbach in a small Lithuanian town, and recalls the friendship formed in South Africa.
body: Seeraj Saxena's travelogue in Samalochan begins at Daugavpils in Latvia, home to the Mark Rothko museum, and passes through Panevėžys and Šiauliai in Lithuania to the hill of Girnikai. On the way there are friends, Dennis, Vaiva and Meta, and the cold light of the Baltic.

The destination is Rusnė, a town on the Atmata river, from where Russian territory is just twenty metres away. Here stands a statue of Gandhi and Hermann Kallenbach, made by Ramūnas Kvintas and unveiled on 2 October 2015. The concept was by architect Gintautas Višniauskas, and the cost was borne by Dr Yusuf K. Hamied, in memory of Luba Derczansky Hamied, who died on 4 April 1991.

Kallenbach was born in 1871, grew up in Rusnė, and from 1896 was an architect in South Africa. There he befriended Gandhi, and Tolstoy Farm stood on the ground of that friendship. He died in 1945 and was buried at Degania.
The essay ends with the author's own poem 'Gandhi in Rusnė', in which this small town and this old friendship come together.
nazar: We often see Gandhi alone, as a symbol. This essay sets him beside a friend, a Jewish architect on whose land Tolstoy Farm was settled.
In this age of hatred, a statue of the friendship of two men of different faiths and continents, twenty metres from the Russian border, is a statement in itself.
sawal: How much room is left for Gandhi's friends in Gandhi's story?
ref: Hermann Kallenbach
A Lithuanian-born Jewish architect who became Gandhi's close friend and collaborator in South Africa. In 1910 he gave his land near Johannesburg for Tolstoy Farm.
Tolstoy Farm
An ashram near Johannesburg where the families of satyagrahis lived together, farmed, and taught and learned among themselves.

h: Dostoevsky: the writer of the mind's cellar
dek: Poet Vijayshankar Chaturvedi writes that Fyodor Dostoevsky placed a camera inside the human head before Freud, and that the gaze of this writer who came back from the gallows still watches us.
body: Vijayshankar Chaturvedi's essay in Samalochan begins with the view of Dostoevsky as a kind of next prophet, and goes on to Raskolnikov of 'Crime and Punishment', inside whose head the writer seems to place a camera.

The essayist reminds us that Dostoevsky was born in 1821 and died in 1881, while Freud was born in 1856. The digging into the mind's cellar that psychoanalysis did later had already been done in literature.

The essay pauses at the most dramatic turn of his life: arrest in 1849 for his links with the Petrashevsky circle, a mock execution at Semyonovsky Square in which the sentence was changed at the last moment, and then Siberia. The experience of seeing death so close returns later in Prince Myshkin of 'The Idiot'.
nazar: To read Dostoevsky is to pass through questions of crime, guilt and forgiveness. In an age when everything is instantly sorted into right and wrong, his tangled humanity is a necessary medicine.
sawal: Can anyone be punished without being fully understood?
ref: Petrashevsky circle
A group of intellectuals in 1840s St Petersburg who debated utopian socialism and reform. Tsar Nicholas I had its members arrested in 1849.
Raskolnikov
The protagonist of 'Crime and Punishment' (1866), a poor student who murders an old pawnbroker and is then broken by his own guilt.

h: Kamini and the gaze of three generations
dek: Pankaj Subeer's new story is about a grandfather, son and grandson who share out, in their imagination, a woman who comes to work in their house, and then avenge their own misunderstanding with abuse.
body: Pankaj Subeer's story 'Kali Kaamnaon ke Collage mein Kamini' (Kamini in a Collage of Dark Desires), published in Janki Pul, is written in the manner of a storyteller, and each section opens with an Urdu couplet. The story is summarised here; the full text can be read on the original page.

Outside the city is a colony called 'Phooti Bijauri', where middle-class people who have retired, or are about to, have settled in their own houses. In one house live three generations, grandfather, son and grandson, and a woman who to these three is only daughter-in-law, wife and mother. There is just one name in the story: Kamini alias Kammo, who comes to work in this house.

From their separate rooms the three men watch Kammo, take her laughter and humming as an invitation meant for them, and begin to pray for each other's absence so as to be alone with her. The satire grows sharper: the woman whose body they stare at has no idea of their intent.

Then one Sunday Kammo does not come. It turns out she has married a lonely man from the same colony in a temple. At the dinner table the three men shower her with abuse and accusations, and that very night events begin in the house that are the fruit of their own 'prayers'.
nazar: This story is an X-ray of the male gaze. Its greatest strength is that it shows the woman not as a victim but as someone who chooses her own life, and the real laughter falls on three men who do not even know her.
Every wrong assumption made in the story about the domestic worker, that being alone makes her 'available', mirrors a society that still looks at working women with suspicion and greed.
sawal: If no one ever asked the woman, why the anger at her own choice?
ref: Qissagoi
The old tradition of storytelling in which the teller speaks directly to the reader, adds comments and embellishes the tale with idioms and couplets.
Pankaj Subeer
A fiction writer and editor from Sehore, Madhya Pradesh, author of novels such as 'Akaal Mein Utsav' and 'Jinhen Jurm-e-Ishq Pe Naaz Tha', and recipient of the Jnanpith Navlekhan award.

h: Poems by Deepankar Gupta: masks, some flowers and a fistful of village
dek: Poems by a young poet born in Araria about the hypocrisy of poets, flowers at the margins, a village being emptied and silence, and in the end a trust that this world will survive.
body: Janki Pul has published nine poems by Deepankar Gupta. The poet was born in 2000 in a village in Bihar's Araria district and now lives in Bhopal, working on screenplays for short films and in graphic design alongside poetry.

The first poem, 'Mukhauta' (Mask), is about writers who speak in their poems of humanity, of Adivasis and of women's freedom, but stand against all this in their lives. 'Kuchh Phool' (Some Flowers) is about flowers never granted the right to be called flowers, which bloom in forests, by drains and in slums, and which will one day demand their share of the earth.

In 'Mutthi Bhar Gaon' (A Fistful of Village), a grandmother's letters emerge from a father's old suitcase, with the whole village written into them: the mango orchard, the footpaths, the bullocks, and people being divided in the name of religion. 'Cheekhen' (Screams) is about women's voices rising from the pages of the newspaper, and 'Bachi Rahegi Yah Duniya' (This World Will Survive) is addressed to a friend who keeps speaking the truth in an age of fear.
nazar: These are poems of honest anger more than of mature craft, and that is their strength. 'Mukhauta' asks Hindi's literary world the question that often goes unasked for fear of big names.
sawal: How much distance between a poet's poems and his life can be forgiven?
ref: Araria
A district in Bihar's Seemanchal region on the Nepal border, from where large numbers of people migrate to other states for work.
Janki Pul
A Hindi literary web magazine edited by Prabhat Ranjan, which publishes fiction, poetry, translation and reviews.

h: Katra's Ramlila: where Ravana is worshipped first
dek: Rashi Pandey writes about a 150-year-old tradition in Allahabad's Katra neighbourhood, where the Ramlila begins with Ravana's procession because he is regarded as the grandson of sage Bharadwaj.
body: Rashi Pandey's essay in Hindwi's Bela section opens with a comic scene. After Covid, Katra prepared for Ravana's procession for the first time in years, but wind and rain attacked so fiercely that the king of Lanka turned back from Azad Chauraha itself. The writer calls it Indra's old revenge.

Then the essay goes into history. Allahabad's Ramlila is said to predate Tulsidas. According to the 'Tabaqat-i-Akbari', while building the fort in 1583 Akbar watched a Ramlila, was moved by the scenes of Rama's exile and Dasharatha's death, and ordered Abul Fazl and Badayuni to translate the Valmiki Ramayana into Persian.

Every large neighbourhood of the city has its own Ramlila committee, but Katra is the only one where Ravana's procession goes out in full splendour on the Ekadashi of Pitru Paksha, after which all of Katra is held to be under Ravana's rule. Ravana is not burnt here, because he is regarded as the grandson of sage Bharadwaj and an ancestor of Katra's people. The burning takes place at Alopibagh together with the Daraganj committee, and people say with true Allahabadi swagger that if not here, he will surely die somewhere else.
nazar: In the same city Ravana is both an ancestor and an effigy to be burnt. The essay reminds us that our traditions are not one but many, and that their strength lies in this plurality. The Ramlila that moved Akbar to have the Ramayana translated is a shared inheritance, nobody's private estate.
sawal: In a city where even Ravana is someone's ancestor, can a single story be imposed?
ref: Tabaqat-i-Akbari
A 16th-century history in Persian by Nizamuddin Ahmad, covering India up to the reign of Akbar.
Ramdal
The procession of Allahabad's Ramlila, in which neighbourhood committees take out tableaux and floats.

h: The fear of being clipped, and the honesty of speaking
dek: In Hindwi's column 'Reel Rasacharya', Rachit asks why, with a camera on every stage, speakers police their own words, and how justified it is to feel hurt when a reel is clipped.
body: Rachit describes three kinds of speakers. The first sugar-coats his words out of fear of the camera and avoids naming names, in other words practises self-censorship, because he fears an hour of talk will become a one-minute clip cut from its context. The second does the opposite, speaking over the top for applause. The third knows that whoever is looking for something will find it, and speaks honestly anyway.
The writer reminds us that this fear is not new. Newspapers used to be accused of twisting statements; now that notoriety falls to those who clip reels.

The essay is a disagreement with a piece by a media teacher who wrote two pages about his distress after his reel went viral. With sympathy, Rachit says that in that reel he had said something important, the full video was available, and sensible viewers form opinions after watching the whole. His conclusion is that one should say what one means with complete honesty and then let happen what will, because the world is neither an institution nor a classroom.
nazar: In a week when journalists standing on the street are being detained, this short essay says something big: speaking out of fear is also a kind of silence. The age of reels can cut anyone out of context, but the remedy is not to speak less but to speak clearly.
sawal: How much more silent will the fear of being taken out of context make us?
ref: Context collapse
The situation on social media in which something said in one context reaches many kinds of unknown audiences and loses its original context.
Self-censorship
When a person censors their own words out of fear, pressure or anticipated consequences, without any external restriction.

h: Thirst in Temru Mal: taps installed, no water
dek: In a Gond and Korku village in Betul, all five hand pumps and three wells dry up as April arrives. Women make seven trips a day, and the taps fitted in every house have yet to give a single drop.
body: Pooja Dhurve, 28, a Gond Adivasi of Temru Mal village in Madhya Pradesh's Betul district, says that as soon as March ends and April begins, all five hand pumps and all three wells in the village dry up completely. Then only one hope remains: a well 800 metres outside the village.

Women make up to seven trips a day, between 5 and 11 in the morning and between 4 and 7 in the evening. In summer the temperature goes up to 45 degrees. According to Pooja one trip takes more than half an hour, longer if there is a crowd; about 200 people draw water from that well. When the water is late, food for the men leaving for daily wage work is late, and children reach school late and get scolded.

The village is largely Gond and Korku Adivasi. A third of the families own 1 to 5 bigha of land, growing paddy and corn for their own use. The rest go through labour contractors to work in construction in Indore, Bhopal and Gujarat. Residents said that, fed up with the water shortage, 15 families left the village before the summer of 2025.

A year ago taps were installed in every house, with a formal inauguration. But according to the villagers, not a single drop of water has come from them to this day. The gram panchayat has been petitioned in writing several times, and the reply is always the same: 'We will do it.' Pooja says, 'Just hearing that we have to go to fetch water makes my eyes fill up.'
nazar: A tap in every house and water in every house are two different things. Temru Mal had its inauguration, the village joined the statistics, and the women's trips stayed exactly where they were.
Water shortage here is not just thirst but a reason for migration. In a village that families leave every year, a dry tap is less the failure of a scheme than the beginning of a village emptying out.
sawal: A tap that has never given water: in which count is it recorded?
ref: Jal Jeevan Mission
A central scheme launched in 2019 that aims to bring piped drinking water to every rural household ('Har Ghar Jal').
Korku
An Adivasi community of the Satpura hills in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, with its own language of the Munda family.

h: Kumbhalgarh: a tiger forced into leopard country
dek: A proposal to turn Rajasthan's Kumbhalgarh sanctuary into a tiger reserve could empty 51 villages inside it. Herders and Adivasis ask: what will a tiger give us?
body: In Ramjigudadhani in Pali district, 65-year-old herder Phuaram shows the leopard's teeth marks on a kid's neck; he beat the animal away with a stick. Then he says, 'Now imagine if that was a tiger.' His wife Matra answers that neither the goat nor he would have survived. This settlement of about 70 families borders the Kumbhalgarh Wildlife Sanctuary, where grazing is the mainstay.

Created in 1971, the 610 sq km sanctuary is a thin strip of scrub forest, in places only four kilometres wide. On 4 August 2023 the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) cleared a proposal to merge it with Todgarh Raoli to create the country's 59th tiger reserve. Around 51 villages inside and 250 on the periphery would be affected. Peesulal Meghwal, the Dalit sarpanch of Guda Jatan, says the Forest Rights Act requires the written consent of the gram sabha, but from 2010 till today the forest department has not held a single meeting with them.

In Kharni Tokri, a Bhil settlement with no electricity, water or school, officials offered ₹15 lakh in cash instead of land, while a bigha near the panchayat road sells for ₹40 lakh. Former forester Mehboob Mohammed says there is no reservoir, no grassland and no prey here; this is the country of the leopard, the nilgai and the wolf. The NTCA's own 2020-21 report records Rajasthan's Chief Wildlife Warden saying Kumbhalgarh is not ideal tiger habitat, yet the same report also notes local support. Rajasthan has 721 of India's 13,874 leopards.

In the 20 years since the tiger news, hotels have grown from four to over a hundred, and land sells in crores. Rajsamand's BJP MP Mahima Kumari Mewar has met Union forest minister Bhupender Yadav twice to demand the plan be revoked. Kumbhalgarh was not mentioned at the NTCA meeting of 9 July 2026. The villagers count it a small win. Hira Ram Sopaji of Garasia Colony says: 'We will die, we will be erased, but we will not leave.'
nazar: The 'fortress conservation' model of saving tigers assumes the forest must be emptied of people, whereas in Kumbhalgarh herders, Bhils and Garasias have lived with the leopard for centuries. The question here is not tiger versus human, but a decision taken behind closed doors.
As in Kaziranga, conservation and tourism seem to move together here: villages go, hotels grow. A claim to save the forest without asking those who know it is hollow.
sawal: In a forest where no tiger has been seen for seventy years, whose room is being made?
ref: Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006

A law that gives Adivasis and traditional forest dwellers individual and community rights over forest land and resources. Under it, the written consent of the gram sabha is required before displacement.
Fortress conservation
A model of conservation that holds that protecting wildlife requires emptying an area of people entirely. The core of a tiger reserve works on this basis.

h: Civilisations built on trade, wary of the trader
dek: Devdutt Pattanaik moves from the Panis of the Rig Veda to China's 'shang' and Manu's interest rates to show that where kings and priests wrote the rules, the merchant was pushed down, and where monks lived on gifts, he was praised.
body: In Sanskrit a trader is a 'vanik', from the root 'pan', to bargain. From the same root come the Panis of the Rig Veda, whom the Vedic poets clearly disliked. In hymn 10.108 the Panis hide cattle in a cave and Indra's dog Sarama is sent to find them. The poets call them stingy, people who do not share. According to Pattanaik, this is where the merchant enters Indian memory as the man who holds back what others want.

In Chinese the merchant is 'shang', also the name of the Shang dynasty the Zhou overthrew around 1046 BCE. One old story says the defeated Shang, stripped of land, took to trade to survive. China ranked people in four groups: scholar, farmer, artisan, merchant. The first Han emperor, Gaozu, banned merchants from wearing silk and riding in carriages and taxed them hard, and then the state ran short of money. In the debate of 81 BCE on the salt and iron monopolies, the Confucian scholars won on morals and the finance minister Sang Hongyang, a merchant's son, won on money. Japan copied the ladder, but by the 1700s Osaka's rice brokers were lending to the lords ranked above them.

India had no single view. The Bhagavad Gita (9.32) calls the Vaishya, like women and Shudras, born of 'papa-yoni', able to reach the highest goal by taking refuge in Krishna; in the writer's words, equality with a queue. According to Pattanaik this prompted many merchant families to adopt a pure vegetarian life to rise up the caste ladder. Manusmriti counts the Vaishya among the twice-born, but in 8.142 sets interest rates by the borrower's caste: 2 percent a month for a Brahmin, 3 for a Kshatriya, 4 for a Vaishya, 5 for a Shudra. Even your loan knows your birth, he writes.

Step outside the Brahmin texts and the mood changes. In Buddhist stories the setthi is a hero: Anathapindika buys the Jetavana grove for the Buddha by covering the ground with gold coins. Jain monks lived almost entirely on the gifts of trading families, who built the temples of Mount Abu and Shatrunjaya. Pattanaik's conclusion: where kings and priests wrote the rules and farming was the main source of income, the merchant was pushed down, because his wealth was a power they could not control. Where monks depended on donors, he was praised.
nazar: This essay is a reminder that the hierarchies written into scripture did not descend from the sky; they came from whoever held the pen. Where the merchant was placed depended on who wrote the rules and where his bread came from.
Today, when big business itself has begun writing the rules of politics, the question is reversed: whom should we now be wary of, and whose hand holds the pen?
sawal: Does whoever writes the rules also decide whose wealth is a sin?
ref: Panis
A community in the Rig Veda described as wealthy but miserly. Hymn 10.108 is a dialogue between Sarama and the Panis.
Anathapindika
A wealthy merchant (setthi) of Shravasti and a leading lay follower of the Buddha, who bought the Jetavana grove from Prince Jeta and gave it to the Sangha.
